The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the time horizon extends, which is entirely expected given how uncertainty compounds over time. Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data, a hawkish surprise from a major central bank, or a sudden risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical tensions could easily breach the lower bound of even the one-month interval. A credit event, liquidity shock, or sharp equity sell-off could amplify these moves. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic print, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical uncertainty could fuel a sharp rally beyond the upper bound.

It is also worth acknowledging that model-based intervals assume relatively stable volatility regimes and historical correlations that may not hold. Tail events, by definition, occur more frequently than standard distributional assumptions suggest, and any structural break in the underlying asset's behavior, such as a sudden change in liquidity conditions or a major institutional flow, could render these intervals overly narrow. Readers should treat the confidence intervals as indicative rather than definitive boundaries, particularly at the one-month horizon where the range of plausible scenarios is especially wide.
